en: The Ritual Manual for the Fire Hūṃ:
The Vidyā of Maheśvara, King of the Northeastern Quarter: NAMAḤ SAMANTABUDDHĀNĀM OṂ I...
Recite "Śanaye Svāhā" seven times. The mantra of Śakra, King of the Gods of the East:
"Namaḥ samantabuddhānām | Oṃ indrāya svāhā. The mantra of Agni, King of the Gods of the Southeast:
"Namaḥ samantabuddhānām | Oṃ agnaye svāhā. The mantra of Yama, King of the Gods of the South:
The mantra of the Heavenly King Nairṛti in the southwest: *Namaḥ samantabuddhānāṃ oṃ jvālamaye svāhā*.
The mantra of the Heavenly King Varuṇa in the west: *Namaḥ samantabuddhānāṃ oṃ rākṣasādhipate svāhā*.
The mantra of the Heavenly King Vāyu in the northwest: *Namaḥ samantabuddhānāṃ oṃ vāruna ye svāhā*.
The mantra of Vaiśravaṇa, King of the North: *Namaḥ samantabuddhānāṃ oṃ vajraye svāhā*.
The mantra of Mahābrahmā above, to the right of Śakra: *Namaḥ samantabuddhānāṃ oṃ yakṣamitranāthāri svāhā*.
*Namo samantabuddhānām oṃ prajñāpate svāhā*. To the left of Jalendra, the King of the Earth-dwelling Devas of the lower direction:
*Namo samantabuddhānām oṃ parajñe svāhā*. To the left of Śakra, the Sun Deva:
*Namo samantabuddhānāṃ oṃ aniyataya svāhā*. To the right of Candradeva (the Moon Deity) is that of Varuṇa:
*Namo samantabuddhānāṃ oṃ jalarāja svāhā*. The mantras for the various stellar deities (*tārakadevatā*) are the same as those for the position of Candradeva.
The mantra of the Nāga Kings, identical to that of the Water Deities, is: *Namaḥ samantabuddhānāṃ oṃ nakṣatratārī vate svāhā*.
The mantras of all the messengers and various spirits (*bhūta*) are to be scattered in the northeast: *Namaḥ samantabuddhānāṃ oṃ megasheṇaye svāhā*.
“Bhibhi bhibhi viśe svāhā | Bhūtānām svāhā. Whenever reciting the mantra of Acala, one must construct a maṇḍala; the method for the maṇḍala is as shown in the illustration below.
One should offer flowers of blue and black colors, burn aloeswood and benzoin incense, and at appropriate times provide seasonal fruits, food and drink, lamps, and scented water as offerings.

When wishing to perform an offering, the practitioner shall bathe and don new garments. First, they should recite the mantra of their chosen deity (iṣṭadevatā) and form the mudrā of that deity. Taking scented water with a ladle, they sprinkle it upon all the offering articles; this is called "purifying protection" (*parirakṣaṇa*), whereby no demons can defile them.
Furthermore, employing the method of offering from the Heart of the Treasury of Space is most inconceivable.
Having completed the arrangement of the offering implements, one should immediately recite the Samaya mantra to expel obstructors and establish the boundary.
To recite the Vairocana Samaya Mantra while seated and binding the mudrā:

"Namaḥ samantabuddhānām oṃ āḥ samaye tṛsamaye samayaye svāhā. This refers to the binding of the Samaya-mudrā by joining the palms; one should place it upon the forehead, the left and right shoulders, the heart, and the throat, reciting the aforementioned mantra once for each location.
Then, forming the seal of Acala, recite the mantra of Acala seven times while circling to the left to expel obstructors;
then recite it three more times while circling to the right to establish the boundary.

Having completed the boundary-binding (*sīmābandha*), one then forms the Hook-seal (*aṅkuśamudrā*) by interlacing the two hands with the right index finger extended upward, and thereby invites all Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, Vajradharas, and others to descend and assemble at the site of practice (*maṇḍala*).
The mantra for the Hook Seal (*ākarṣaṇamudrā*) is:

*Namaḥ samantabuddhānāṃ sarvatra-pratihata-hṛdaya-tathāgatāṅkuśa-pāriplu-loka-svāhā*. Recite this once for each hook; after three hooks have been cast, visualize that all Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, and immeasurable assemblies of holy ones descend and gather together. Then, having sat down, perform prostrations, repentance, the making of vows, and the declaration of what you seek.

Thereafter, bind the Vairocana Heart Seal: interlace the ring and little fingers; extend the middle fingers and bend their upper joints so that their tips touch one another; slightly bend the index fingers and place their tips against the sides of the upper joints of the middle fingers; and interlace the thumbs externally. Recite the five-syllable mantra as follows.
The mantra for Vairocana’s subduing of the four māras, liberation from the six realms of existence, and fulfillment of the knowledge of all-knowledge (sarvajñājñāna) is:

“ĀḤ VĪRA HŪṂ KHAṂ. Facing the honored image, form the aforementioned mudrā and recite this mantra seven times. Then, holding a rosary, recite it one hundred times up to one thousand times; the more, the better.
Thereafter, form the mudrā of Acala, which is the sword-mudrā, and recite the mantra of Acala as follows:

*Namo samantabhadra vajranṛtya mahāruṣṇa sarvaduṣṭān trāsaya hūṃ traṭ phaṭ maṃ* Facing the image of the Honored One, form the aforementioned mudrā and recite this mantra seven times. Thereafter, holding a rosary, recite it one hundred times, or even up to one thousand times; the more, the better.
Having completed the recitation, one must further form the mudrā of the principal deity and again recite the mantra seven times.
After diligently making vows and prostrating, one should once more form the aforementioned samaya-mudrā and recite the samaya-mantra three times.

Furthermore, having bound the sword mudrā and rotated it once counter-clockwise to dissolve the boundary, visualize that the assembly of holy ones each returns to their respective lands, and then exit the maṇḍala.
Whether walking, standing, sitting, or reclining, maintain the recitation of the mantra of the principal deity in mind without interruption.
The Mantra for Offering Food to Acala:

*Namo samantabhadra vajranātha traṭa am mū ga jñā ma ha ru svaraṇa sarvatra tra ya hūṃ trāma ya trāma ya hūṃ trāṭa phaṭ* One should always set aside one portion of every meal to offer as an oblation, reciting this mantra once. By doing so, one will always receive protection in all places.
The Mantra for Bathing:
“Oṃ jhuḥ sarva-ha. Take one scoop of water, recite the preceding mantra seven times over it, and sprinkle that scoop of water upon your body; this shall serve as your bath.

As previously described for the offering of food to the eight directions, take beans, fruits, cakes, cooked rice, sesame seeds, non-glutinous rice, powdered unguents, various flowers, and so forth; mix them with water and place them in a flask or basin, then scatter them in the four directions with a joyful heart as an offering to the devas and spirits.
The unguents, powdered incense, and their attendants are each bestowed with their respective mantras.
The mantra of Īśāna, the Deva of the Northeast, is:
Oṃ īśānāya svāhā. The mantra of Śakra, the Deva of the East, is:
"Oṃ indrāye svāhā. The mantra of the Fire Deity (Agni) in the southeast is:
"Oṃ agnaye svāhā. The mantra of King Yama in the east is: "Oṃ yamāya svāhā. The mantra of the Rākṣasas in the southwest is:
"Oṃ rakṣā-pratīye svāhā. This is the mantra of the various nāgas and water deities of the western direction.
"Oṃ vārunaye svāhā. This is the mantra of the various wind deities of the northwest.
"Oṃ vāyave svāhā. This is the mantra of the various yakṣas of the northern direction.
“Oṃ yakṣa-bhijidya-pataye svāhā. The mantra for bestowing upon the various classes of spirits and deities in the upper direction is:
“Oṃ iṅgini-maṃsani-pūta-namaḥ svāhā. The mantra for the lower direction is: “Oṃ bhiñji bhiñji viśeṣa-ccha-namaḥ svāhā.

Having performed the ritual offerings as described above, one should wash the hands and rinse the mouth, re-enter the maṇḍala, prostrate to the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, and perform recitation as usual.
“You who are the celestial protector, Who have practiced supreme conduct Under the Buddhas, the Guides,
And purified the stages and the perfections;
Just as the Lion of the Śākyas, the Savior of the World, Routed the hosts of Māra.”
"I too have subdued Māra; I draw the maṇḍala.
*Namo samantabuddhānām oṃ pṛthivīye svāhā.* In the *Homa-vidhi*, one scroll: Regarding the ritual of *homa*, one should contemplate the syllable "Laṃ" as the bodhicitta.
The resident first invites the Fire Deity, saying:
"I now respectfully invite the foremost of fire deities, the sage within fire;
having first paid homage, please descend upon this seat and accept the homa offering."
The mantra for requesting the Fire Deity (Agni) is:

*Namaḥ samantabuddhānām oṃ agnaye svāhā*. Furthermore, the mudrā and mantra of the Fire Deity follow the fundamental [deity’s] mudrā, with the sole modification that the two middle fingers are bent into the shape of a half-ring, ensuring their tips do not touch.
This is the single Dharma-seal; it is used to summon the Fire Deity (Agnideva) for offerings.
When the offerings have been completed and one dismisses the Fire Deity, one then extends the tips of the two middle fingers.
The mudrā-mantra is:
*Namaḥ vāgīśvarāya aihi ehi tiṣṭha mama hṛdi svāhā*. This one-seal mantra is for the food offering to the Fire God (*Agnideva*).

During these three rounds, one first requests the Fire Deity (Agni) to burn the food for offering, and subsequently burns the food as an offering to the Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, Vajras, and various secret mantras.
The mantra of the Fire Deity is:
Oṃ āgneye hūṃ svāhā svāhā vāgīśvara yaḥ svāhā. When the ritual is completed, one should dismiss the Fire Deity using the aforementioned mantra and mudrā of the Fire Deity.

regarding the *Huìyùn* (Rhyme Collection) entry for the phonetic glosses of the *Huìxū Yíguǐ* (Ritual Manual of the Seed-Syllable HŪṂ):
"Ding" (pronounced with the *li* final).
The *Shuowen Jiezi*: "Clarity."
Xu Riguang said, "Indeed so.
The *Zengyun* states:
"It means reality; it also means the ultimate point."
Furthermore, "dìng" (with the fanqie reading jī) signifies a distant appearance or clear vision.
It is also written as "zì," meaning clarity or understanding.
"Cuì" (with the fanqie reading qīng suì) means easily broken.
Regarding "fragrant crisp cakes": these are likely the Hu-style crisp cakes (*hu-cuibing*).
As for "placing them in a steamer to make a lid," this refers to the *jǐng* and *yù* steamed cakes and similar varieties.
*Pán* (pronounced *bùgān*) means a tray or platter.
*Dian* (dàojiàn fǎn) means to settle, to place, to present, to arrange, and to adjust.
*Dou* (dòudòu fǎn) is a name for a measure.
The *Erya* states:
"It is a food vessel.
Today, it is placed with the upper and lower parts joined together.
*Zhuàn* (zhuàn, upper tone) means food and drink.
*Fēn* (fú yún, second tone) means fragrant harmony.
*Pō* (pǔ jiā, first tone) refers to the white color of grass flowers.
Furthermore, it is the character "páng" (皅).
Now, "shàngxià hé" (上下合) means "to combine the upper and lower.
"Yán bèibèi" (嚴被被) means "to be fully prepared."
Because they share the same pronunciation, one is used in place of the other.
"Bǎo" (珤) is an archaic form of the character "bǎo" (寶).
"Cān" (餐) is pronounced as *qiān* and *dān*, or *qiān* and *cāng*; it means to swallow.
To receive emolument without merit is called "idle consumption" (sùcān).
*Kù* (酷) is pronounced with the initial *g* reversed; it means "to ripen.
*Liè* (烈) is pronounced with the initial *l* reversed; it means "majestic power" (*wēiyè*).
To say that the fruits flourish in emptiness is called "cruelty" (kùliè).
The character for "low" (dī) is pronounced with the initial *jī* and final *-āng*.
The character for "clod" (kuài) has two pronunciations: *kǒuqīng* and *kǒuhuí*.
*Ki* (堛): the phonetic component is *bi* (逼) with the tone *shàn* (善).
*Lú* (瀘): the phonetic component is *lǚ* (屢) with the tone *fú* (浮). *Zǐ* (滓):
the phonetic component is *wǔ* (武) with the tone *yě* (也).
*Jingzi* (semen) means pure, good, bright, virtuous, and correct.
*Mo-poda* (pronounced with the second tone on *po*) and *pójie* (pronounced with the second tone on *jie*) mean gruel.
*Mí* (糜) refers to the inner skin [of grain] and is a thick gruel (*zhān*).
*Dài* (䄞) means to be crushed into *mí*; *jī* (𮂦), pronounced *zhǐ*, means to be broken into pieces, the chaff, or the refined essence.
Today, it is sometimes written as "mí."
*Chāo* (pronounced *chū jiào*) means to plunder or to take by force.
*Sà* (pronounced *sū hàn*) refers to a type of cake made from parched rice; it is also written as "rǎo" or "shà. It is a sweetened rice dish.
It is also written as "shà."
"Lùdòu" (菉豆): the first character is pronounced as "lù.
It refers to *wángchū* (王芻).
"Yūnyù" (熅郁): the second character is pronounced as "yù," meaning smoky fumes; it refers to smoke that is thick with vapor.
*Bó* (pronounced with the *pú-mò* rhyme) means robustness and flourishing.
*Shàngfǔcūbāolǚ* refers to the upper part; *xiàhèwǔlǚ* refers to the lower part.
*Bào* (pronounced with both the *bójiào* and *pǔjué* rhymes) refers to the skin being scattered and raised.
*Zhà* (pronounced with the *dù* and *jià* finals) means to spray.
The upper part is *pā tuó míng qū*, and the lower part is *nǎng lóu*.
*Chóu* refers to those of the same true category or kind.
*Kè* (pronounced with the *wò* rhyme) means to admonish.
*Bǐng* (pronounced with the *bǐ* rhyme) means to grasp.
*Lèi* (pronounced with the *lì* rhyme) refers to the sections of silk.
*Nei* (pronounced with the *jie* tone) means to press down or constrain.
There are three types of fire altars:
first, for peace and security; second, for prosperity; and third, for the removal of enemies.

First, to ensure stability, one should prepare a ritual platform in an open space; in its center, depict the Buddha seated upon a lotus throne, and on the four sides of the platform, depict Prajñāpāramitā Bodhisattva, the Śrāvakas, and Maitreya Bodhisattva.
Paint the marks and signs of the Buddha’s physical form.
Paint one crescent moon, and further paint the Ābhāsvara Pure Abode Heaven and the Dragon King; within the mandala, make offerings of incense and flowers.
In the southwest corner of the maṇḍala, construct a fire altar four finger-widths high.
Within it, excavate a square hearth one cubit on each side, and smear white earth upon the center of the furnace.
The altar is four finger-widths high, with a rim one finger-width wide; within it, burn mulberry wood, *kautaka* wood, or persimmon wood, each piece being one span (*vitasti*) in length.
Select the thick ends of the branches, smear both ends with ghee, honey, and curd, and burn them one by one while reciting the mantra once for each.
Take barley, wheat, ghee, honey, curd, and milk; recite the mantra once over each and burn them.
Perform this one thousand and eight times.
Do this at each of the three periods of the day for seven days, or for half a month, or a month, and [the affliction] will immediately cease and become tranquil.
Wearing fresh white garments, one should perform recitations within the mandala and then carry out the fire-offering ritual within the fire-altar.
Beginning on the first day of the month, one performs the rite at dusk; at that time, the Śuddhāvāsa deities assemble, and the method for attaining peace and security is accomplished.

Facing north, sit upon a mat of *māṭi* grass in the full lotus posture (*paryaṅka*). Light a fire altar and perform offerings of clay, incense, and flowers at the three periods of the day. Once the offerings have been made, use incense that is naturally free of thorns for worship; one will immediately eliminate all calamities and misfortunes, attain longevity, and be cured of all diseases. Should any strange or ominous transformations occur, perform this rite in every instance.
Next, the ritual for the fire altar of Abundance is explained.

If one wishes to perform the fire ritual, one must first prepare and consecrate an altar. In the center, one should depict the Buddha, Avalokiteśvara, Mahāsthāmaprāpta, and the various great bodhisattvas; as well as Brahmā, Mañjuśrī, the various great yakṣas, the sages, Mahātejas, Hārītī, and so forth. One should then make offerings to them upon this altar.

This rite begins on the fifteenth day. At the time when the sun is about to set, one should sit facing east upon a circular mat of *kuśa* grass in the *paryaṅka* (cross-legged) posture, wearing clean garments and generating a mind of joy.
At this time, when the devas assemble and that person performs the rite, the devas will rejoice and he shall immediately attain accomplishment.

Outside this maṇḍala, on the southern side, construct a large maṇḍala two cubits square. Its base should be two finger-widths wide; dig the earth one cubit deep, and the central altar should be one span wide and four finger-widths high.

Using a mandala of red earth, one should make offerings of lotus fragrance within the altar; one may burn incense made from wood, milk-rice porridge, ghee, and curd, or alternatively, sesame seeds mixed with rice is also acceptable.
Three times each day, perform one thousand and eight recitations for each session.

As for the wooden splinters, take branches from a tree as thick as a finger; smear both ends with ghee, honey, milk, and curd, and burn them one by one while reciting the mantra. Do this one thousand and eight times, or one hundred and eight times, for either seven days or half a month.
By performing the ritual in this manner, the rite will be accomplished.
This concludes the third exposition on the method for the *Vajra-āgneya-maṇḍala* (the Fire Altar for Subduing Enemies).

If one wishes to perform the rite for subduing enemies with fire, one should do so on the eighth or fifteenth day of the dark fortnight, or at midnight; for it is at these times that all malevolent spirits, yakṣas, and rākṣasas assemble. At that time, one should construct a triangular altar (*maṇḍala*), facing south. Using black earth, one should sweep the altar to a size of one cubit (*hasta*) in length, three finger-breadths in height, and two finger-breadths in width. In the center, one should place a trident and take donkey dung, camel dung, and ashes—using these three substances to plaster the altar.
If one has an enemy who causes distress or harbors a mind of malice, one should immediately perform this rite.

One should wear red or blue garments, or alternatively, perform a great malevolent rite by taking blood to dye one’s clothes. Squatting in the Hu fashion, trample with the feet, face westward, frown, glare with bared teeth, hold the body upright and straight, and with a focused mind, utter the words of the mantra from the altar.

One may also take bran mixed with mustard seeds; three times each day, one should smear the altar with mud. Upon that altar, one takes thorny wood from the *nāga-gandhā* flower to kindle a fire by twirling it, and uses *kṛtavedhana* wood to smear the altar.
One may also take rice husks mixed with mustard seeds, or one's own blood mixed [with them], reciting the mantra once for each burn, performing this one thousand and eight times.

Three times a day, at each session, one should likewise burn human bone, hair, and other such substances, while making a vow of wrath, reciting the mantra once for each burn and calling out the name of the person.

This is the method for subduing enemies: it causes the adversary to suffer from chronic illness, lose their wealth and property, die with blood flowing from the body, have the joints of the body fall apart, and become loathsome to behold.
Furthermore, it describes the method for the Universal Fire Altar (*sarvāgnimaṇḍala*).

It is sixteen finger-widths deep and thirty-two finger-widths wide. A wheel (*cakra*) is placed on the eastern side; three tridents (*triśūla*) on the southern side; a nāga on the western side; a vajra on the northern side; and a lotus (*padma*) is placed in the center.
The remaining offerings should be performed according to the previous procedure; furthermore, one must begin on the day of the Mars star.
Next, the methods for the seals (mudrās) of the various fire deities are explained.
Following that, the seals of the various fire spirits are explained.
Next, the timing for accomplishment is explained.
If one performs the rite during the five months [of the rainy season], rain will certainly fall.
If one performs the rite during the three months [of the dry season], various obstacles will certainly manifest.
If one performs the rite during the first month, various obstacles will certainly arise.
If one performs the rite during the ninth month, sudden thunder and lightning will certainly occur.
All such months must be the fifteenth day; when these signs appear, success is certain.
If one performs rites for stability, one should use the fifteenth, seventh, third, or thirteenth days of each respective month; such days as these are all days of the Ghost Star (Kṛttikā).

Furthermore, the times of solar and lunar eclipses are the most supreme; in the second, third, tenth, and eleventh months, one should perform rites for prosperity and abundance; in the fourth and fifth months, one should perform rites for subduing enemies.
